question_text: Step 1. Initial discussions and application for assessment We will confirm the process with the competent authority and provide additional information on the requirements for an equivalence assessment as needed. Following initial discussions, the competent authority can apply for assessment. A questionnaire is sent to the competent authority requesting information about the regulation of the bivalve mollusc production and processing system. Note: Where an existing certification arrangement exists between the national competent authority in the exporting country and either the US or a member state of the EU, an equivalence assessment may not be required if the bivalves to be exported to Australia will be sourced from areas covered by these existing arrangements. If this applies, the competent authority should provide information on the existing arrangements.

Step 2. Equivalence assessment process The questionnaire is completed and submitted by the competent authority. Once prioritised on our work program, we will assess the information provided and determine whether equivalence has been demonstrated. Additional information or clarification may be required during this process. An on-site audit may be required to verify equivalence. A draft assessment report is provided to the competent authority for comment before the assessment is finalised.

Step 3. Negotiation of certificate A foreign government certification arrangement and foreign government certificate is negotiated if equivalence is determined. Food covered by the certificate can now be imported into Australia.

Jurisdictions wanting to export bivalve molluscs and bivalve mollusc products to Australia can apply for assessment of whether their bivalve mollusc production and processing system provides an equivalent food safety outcome to the system in Australia. If the jurisdiction can meet Australia’s [biosecurity requirements](https://www.awe.gov.au/biosecurity-trade/import/online-services/bicon) and demonstrate equivalence for managing food safety risks, a government certification arrangement will be established to facilitate trade. As part of negotiating certification arrangements, recognition will be given to establishments that are permitted to export to countries that have equivalent shellfish sanitation programs and competent authority oversight as Australia. This includes the United States and member states of the European Union. Consistent with the Codex Alimentarius guideline – Principles for Food Import and Export Inspection and Certification ([CXG 20-1995](http://www.fao.org/fao-who-codexalimentarius/codex-texts/guidelines/en/)), Australia will be open and transparent when determining equivalence. Australia has laws requiring the disclosure of information in certain circumstances. The details of these requirements can be provided. If any information you provide cannot be disclosed, provide this information on separate documentation and an explanation of why the information must not be disclosed. Reasons would include commercial-in-confidence and government-in-confidence. The purpose of this part is to determine whether the control programs for the production, transport and processing of bivalve molluscs are equivalent to that in Australia. Relevant Australian requirements [Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code – Standard 4.2.1 – Primary Production and Processing Standard for Seafood](https://www.legislation.gov.au/Series/F2012L00291) – Clauses 3, 7, 13 and 16

Documented food safety control system for primary production, transport and processing of bivalve molluscs Objective: For Taiwan to provide information on how it regulates to control food safety hazards at all stages of bivalve mollusc production, transport and processing. What documented food safety control system must a business have in place for: producing bivalve molluscs transporting bivalve molluscs processing bivalve molluscs.

The purpose of this part is to determine whether the primary production of bivalve molluscs in Taiwan is equivalent to that in Australia. Relevant Australian requirements * [Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code – Standard 4.2.1 – Primary Production and Processing Standard for Seafood](https://www.legislation.gov.au/Series/F2012L00291) – Clauses 4 to 16 Classifying and monitoring harvest areas Objective: For Taiwan to demonstrate how it regulates to ensure harvest areas are appropriately classified and monitored, for control of microbiological and chemical hazards, to ensure the safety of bivalve molluscs. What regulatory controls apply to ensure bivalve mollusc harvest areas are appropriately classified and monitored? Specify the regulatory controls that apply to ensure bivalve molluscs are only harvested from areas classified as suitable for producing bivalve molluscs and are open at the time of harvesting. What regulatory controls apply to ensure bivalve molluscs are only relayed when the level of contamination can be reduced to safe levels for human consumption without further processing? What regulatory controls apply to ensure bivalve molluscs are safe for human consumption after depuration and pathogenic microorganisms are reduced to an acceptable level? What regulatory controls apply to minimise contamination of bivalve molluscs during handling? What regulatory controls apply to ensure inputs do not affect the safety and suitability of bivalve molluscs? What regulatory controls apply to ensure bivalve molluscs are stored under conditions that do not affect the safety and suitability of the bivalve molluscs, including wet storage at on-land facilities? What regulatory controls apply to ensure bivalve molluscs are transported under conditions that do not affect the safety and suitability of the bivalve molluscs, including being stored under temperature control and monitored for temperature control, where relevant? What regulatory controls apply to ensure packaging for bivalve molluscs is fit for its intended use and will not contaminate the bivalve molluscs? Specify the monitoring and records that must be kept to verify controls are implemented. What regulatory controls apply to ensure the identification, holding and separation of bivalve molluscs for destruction, return or recall? Specify the monitoring and records that must be kept to verify controls are implemented. What regulatory controls apply to ensure businesses take all reasonable measures to only accept bivalve molluscs that are safe and suitable? What regulatory control measures apply to ensure bivalve mollusc handlers have adequate skills and knowledge of food safety and food hygiene to handle bivalve molluscs? Specify the monitoring and records that must be kept to verify these measures are implemented. What regulatory controls apply to ensure the hygienic production of bivalve molluscs, so they do not become unsafe or unsuitable?

Harvesting Objective: For Taiwan to demonstrate how it regulates to ensure bivalve molluscs are only harvested from areas that have been classified as suitable for producing bivalve molluscs for human consumption and were open at the time of harvesting. Relaying Objective: For Taiwan to demonstrate how it regulates relaying to ensure the safety of bivalve molluscs. Depuration Objective: For Taiwan to demonstrate how it regulates to ensure bivalve molluscs are safe for human consumption after depuration. Handling Objective: For Taiwan to demonstrate how it regulates the handling of bivalve molluscs to control potential food safety and food suitability problems that are caused by contamination at all stages of primary production. Inputs Objective: For Taiwan to demonstrate how it regulates to provide assurance that inputs do not adversely affect the safety and suitability of the bivalve molluscs. Storage Objective: For Taiwan to demonstrate how it regulates to control hazards that could be introduced during storage of bivalve molluscs. Transport Objective: For Taiwan to demonstrate how it regulates to control hazards that could arise during transport and delivery of bivalve molluscs. Packaging Objective: For Taiwan to demonstrate how it regulates to control hazards that could arise when bivalve molluscs are packed. Disposal Objective: For Taiwan to demonstrate how it regulates to control hazards that could arise from unsafe or unsuitable bivalve molluscs contaminating those that are safe and suitable. Receipt and traceability Objective: For Taiwan to demonstrate how it regulates to: ensure businesses take all reasonable measures to only accept bivalve molluscs that are safe and suitable ensure businesses can trace movement of bivalve molluscs enabling the businesses to identify and locate bivalve molluscs if recalled because of a safety problem. What regulatory control measures apply to ensure traceability of bivalve molluscs is maintained throughout the supply chain? Specify the monitoring and records that must be kept to verify this measure is implemented. Health and hygiene requirements Objective: For Taiwan to demonstrate how it regulates to ensure the hygienic production of bivalve molluscs, so they do not become unsafe or unsuitable: Premises and equipment
Bivalve mollusc handlers Objective: For Taiwan to demonstrate how it regulates to ensure that bivalve mollusc handlers have appropriate skills and knowledge in bivalve mollusc safety and hygiene.

Objective: For Taiwan to demonstrate how it regulates to ensure that businesses use premises and equipment that are clean and are designed, constructed, maintained and operated so as to produce safe and suitable bivalve molluscs.

What regulatory control measures apply to ensure businesses use premises and equipment that result in the hygienic handling of bivalve molluscs? Specify the monitoring and records that must be kept to verify these measures are implemented.

area | an area where bivalve molluscs are grown or harvested. | batch | a quantity of bivalve molluscs harvested from a particular harvesting area (e.g., marine farm, lease or designated wild shellstock harvest area) and with the same harvest date. | bivalve molluscs | clams, cockles, mussels, oysters, pipi and scallops. | bivalve mollusc handler | a person who engages in or supervises the primary production of bivalve molluscs, for a business. | bivalve mollusc products | foods containing any bivalve molluscs (for example, frozen meals that contain bivalve molluscs as an ingredient), but exclude those that are:   * dried (not semi-dried); and * both retorted and shelf stable. | business | a business, enterprise or activity that involves the primary production of bivalve molluscs intended for sale. | competent authority | the government authority or official body authorised by the government that is responsible for the setting of regulatory food safety requirements and/or for the organisation of official controls including enforcement. | depuration | a process using a controlled environment to reduce the level of certain pathogenic  organisms that may be present in live shellfish. | temperature control | maintaining bivalve molluscs at a temperature of:   1. 5°C, or below if this is necessary to minimise the growth of infectious or toxigenic microorganisms in the food so that the microbiological safety of the food will not be adversely affected for the time the food is at that temperature; or 2. another temperature – if the business demonstrates that maintenance of the food at this temperature for the period of time for which it will be so maintained, will not adversely affect the microbiological safety of the food. |

ready-to-eat bivalve molluscs or bivalve mollusc products in which growth of *Listeria monocytogenes* will not occur | 1. the bivalve molluscs or bivalve molluscs products have a pH less than 4.4 regardless of water activity; or 2. the bivalve molluscs or bivalve molluscs products have a water activity less than 0.92 regardless of pH; or 3. the bivalve molluscs or bivalve molluscs products have a pH less than 5.0 in combination with a water activity of less than 0.94; or 4. the bivalve molluscs or bivalve molluscs products have a refrigerated shelf life no greater than 5 days (includes frozen bivalve molluscs that have a refrigerated shelf life of no greater than 5 days once thawed); or 5. the bivalve molluscs or bivalve molluscs products are frozen (stored and sold frozen to be thawed by the consumer immediately before consumption); or 6. it has been be validated that the level of *Listeria monocytogenes* will not increase by greater than 0.5 log cfu/g over the stated shelf life of the bivalve molluscs or bivalve mollusc products. | food safety control system | the exporting country’s laws and systems for regulating and enforcing bivalve mollusc and bivalve mollusc product production and processing. | foodborne disease | a disease that is likely to be transmitted through consumption of contaminated food. | growing area | a marine or enclosed body of water (i.e. bay, harbour, gulf, cove, lagoon, inlet, estuary or river) in which commercial species of bivalve molluscs grow naturally or are grown by means of aquaculture. A growing area may consist of one or more harvest areas. | harvest area | an area that has been designated by a competent authority for the purpose of growing and/or harvesting commercial quantities of shellstock and may include wildstock or aquacultured shellstock. | harvesting | the capture or taking of bivalve molluscs and includes the capture or taking of bivalve molluscs from an enclosure or pond used in aquaculture. | inputs | any feed, chemicals or other substances used in, or in connection with, the primary production of bivalve molluscs. | premises | any premises including land, vehicles, parts of structures, tents, stalls and other temporary structures, vessels, pontoons, and any other place declared by the competent authority to be a premises, kept or used for the primary production of bivalve molluscs (exclusively or otherwise), regardless of whether the premises are owned by the proprietor, including premises used principally as a private dwelling. |

primary production of seafood, including bivalve molluscs | 1. growing, cultivation, picking, harvesting, collection or catching of seafood; or 2. growing on of seafood; or 3. transportation or delivery of seafood; or 4. holding of live seafood;   and includes processing of seafood. |

processing of seafood, including bivalve molluscs | 1. the killing, dismembering, filleting or cutting into portions, gill or gutting, or skinning of seafood; and 2. the depuration of shellfish and crustaceans; and 3. the shucking or peeling of seafood; and 4. the cooking, including steaming or boiling, of crustaceans; and 5. the brining of seafood; and 6. the packing, treating, washing, freezing, refrigeration or storing of seafood; and 7. other similar activities. | relaying | the transfer of bivalve molluscs from one area to another for the reduction of contaminants in the bivalve molluscs. | sanitary survey | the (written) evaluation of all actual and potential pollution sources and environmental factors which may affect shellfish harvest area water quality and hence the shellfish. | seafood | all aquatic vertebrates and aquatic invertebrates intended for human consumption, but excludes amphibians, mammals, reptiles, and aquatic plants. | shellstock | live shellfish in the shell. | shoreline survey | a survey conducted by a competent authority to identify and record pollution sources within the catchment of a shellfish growing area which contaminate or have the potential to contaminate the water quality of a shellfish harvest area. |
